chapters.title: Chapter 1: From Power Law to Portfolio Strategy

lessons.title: Setting a Portfolio Loss Ratio and Realistic Return Expectations

body.text: Most angels do not quit because their portfolio failed. They quit in year two, when the losses have shown up but the winner has not, because nobody told them that was exactly what a healthy portfolio is supposed to look like at that point.

children.text: The last two lessons built the math of how a portfolio's return gets made: a small number of positions carrying most of the MOIC, and a position count chosen to give that outlier a real chance of showing up. This lesson turns that math into expectations you can actually hold onto when the losses start arriving, which they will, well before the winners do. Get the loss ratio and the timeline wrong in your head, and you will very plausibly abandon a portfolio that was working exactly as designed.
The Loss Ratio You Should Actually Expect

markDefs.definition: The share of positions in a portfolio that return less than the capital invested in them, typically split further into total losses (0x) and partial or breakeven outcomes (roughly 1x).

children.text: In the illustrative 20-startup portfolio from Lesson 1, 15 of 20 positions, three quarters, returned 1x or less. That is not a bad outcome for that portfolio, it is close to the

you should expect at this stage of risk. If you go in expecting most of your positions to work out, and only some of your positions actually deliver, you have set yourself up to feel like the strategy is failing at exactly the moment it is on track.

body.text: If your realised loss ratio after several years looks unusually low, well under 30 to 40%, it is worth asking why, rather than assuming skill. Two common explanations are more likely than exceptional stock-picking: the portfolio is simply too young for its failures to have shown up yet (the subject of the next section), or the positions being backed are systematically later-stage and safer than genuine early-stage risk, which also caps how large the eventual winners can be.

children.text: The J-Curve: Why Early Years Look Worse Than They Are

Failures and winners do not arrive on the same timeline. A startup that is not going to work usually reveals that within 18 to 36 months, it runs out of runway, cannot raise its next round, or simply stalls. A startup that is going to work often needs 5 to 10 years to reach an exit that actually returns cash. This mismatch produces what is commonly called a J-curve: a portfolio's marked value tends to dip in its early years as failures get written down faster than winners get written up, then climbs later as the survivors mature and exits start returning real cash.

events.title: Failures Surface First
events.description: The weakest positions run out of runway or fail to raise their next round. This is where the loss ratio becomes visible, well before any winners have matured.

events.title: Signal Emerges
events.description: Surviving positions raise growth rounds at higher valuations. Early markups begin, and follow-on decisions from Chapter 4 start to matter.

events.title: Exits Begin
events.description: The first real cash starts coming back through acquisitions, secondary sales, or occasionally an IPO.

events.title: Portfolio Matures
events.description: Most of the portfolio's realised return is now known. A small number of positions typically account for most of it.

children.text: Translating MOIC into IRR: Why the Same Multiple Means Different Things

A 3.7x MOIC sounds like one number, but whether it is a good return depends entirely on how long it took. As a simplified approximation, treating a portfolio as a single lump sum invested and a single lump sum returned n years later, the annualised return works out to the multiple raised to the power of 1 over the holding period, minus one.

body.caption: n = years held. This is a simplification: real portfolios have cash going out and coming back across many different years, not one lump sum in and one lump sum out, so an actual XIRR calculation on real cash flow dates will differ from this approximation.
The same 3.7x MOIC at different holding periods

body.text: A 3.7x sounds impressive as a headline multiple, but if it takes 10 years to arrive, the annualised return is roughly 14%, not dramatically different from a long-run equity index return, despite carrying far more risk and total illiquidity for a decade. The multiple tells you how much you made. The holding period tells you whether it was actually worth doing.

body.title: Translate the Lesson 2 Practice Portfolio Into IRR
body.prompt: The 10-startup portfolio from the previous lesson's practice exercise returned a 2.8x MOIC. If the average holding period across its positions was 6 years, what is the approximate IRR? Answer in percent, e.g. 20.0 for 20.0%.
body.explanation: IRR ≈ 2.8^(1/6) − 1 ≈ 1.187 − 1 = 0.187, or about 18.7%. Even a smaller multiple can carry a respectable IRR if it is realised over a shorter period, which is exactly why holding period and multiple have to be read together, never one without the other.

children.text: Benchmarking Against What Else You Could Do With the Money

Angel investing should not be benchmarked against a bank fixed deposit or even against a debt fund, the risk profiles are not remotely comparable. The more honest comparison is against what the same capital could have earned in listed Indian equities, where a position in an NSE or BSE-listed stock can be sold on any trading day through a broker like Zerodha, versus a startup cheque that is locked up for years with no ready buyer at all.

stats.label: Reasonable Angel Portfolio Target
stats.context: Illiquid for 7-10 years, high idiosyncratic risk, wide dispersion of outcomes

body.text: The Nifty 50 long-run CAGR figure above is illustrative and approximate. It moves meaningfully depending on the exact start and end dates chosen, since equity index returns are highly sensitive to the period measured. Check a current, sourced figure before using it in any real comparison or client-facing material.

The gap between the Nifty benchmark and a reasonable angel portfolio target is the illiquidity and risk premium you should demand for tying up capital for a decade in businesses that can go to zero without warning. If your realistic, loss-ratio-adjusted expected IRR is not comfortably above what listed Indian equities could plausibly deliver over the same period, the extra risk and the 7 to 10 year lock-up are very likely not worth it.

children.text: Setting Your Own Loss Ratio Target, Not Just Enduring One

Write down your expected loss ratio and your target blended IRR before you write your first cheque, not after your first few failures. Chapter 5 builds this into a full personal investment policy statement, but the habit starts here: a number on paper, set while you are calm, is what stops you from making an emotional decision to quit the strategy in year two, exactly when the shots-on-goal math from the previous lesson needs you to keep going.

body.title: Eighteen Months In, Four Write-Offs
body.scenario: You started angel investing 18 months ago. You have made 8 investments so far, out of a planned 20. Four of the eight have already shut down and returned nothing. You feel like you are bad at this and are considering stopping.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's framework, what would you actually check before deciding whether to stop?
body.modelAnswer: A 50% loss rate at 8 positions, 18 months in, is close to the illustrative loss ratio this lesson describes for a full, mature portfolio, not a sign of unusual failure. The real questions to check are: is 18 months even enough time for any winner to have shown real signal yet, given the J-curve typically bottoms around year 2 to 3; are the remaining positions still too early to judge; and was the original plan to reach roughly 20 positions, meaning only 8 of the planned shots on goal have been taken so far, well short of the count needed for a reasonable chance of catching an outlier. Stopping now, on the loss ratio alone, would very plausibly mean quitting exactly at the trough of the J-curve, before the strategy has had time to work.

points: A loss ratio of roughly 65 to 80% at or below 1x is not a failing portfolio, it is close to the expected shape for genuine early-stage risk
Failures typically surface years before winners mature, producing a J-curve where a portfolio looks worst well before it looks best
The same MOIC implies very different annualised returns depending on holding period, so multiple and time have to be read together
Angel returns should be benchmarked against liquid alternatives like listed Indian equities plus a real illiquidity and risk premium, not against fixed deposits
Set your expected loss ratio and target IRR in writing before investing, so early losses do not trigger quitting right when the strategy most needs more shots on goal
